On file deletions. We’ve investigated a handful of reports where GPT-5.6 unexpectedly deleted files. What we have found is that this most commonly occurs when: - Full access mode is enabled and codex is run without sandboxing protections, including without auto review being enabled - The model attempts to override the $HOME env var to define a temporary directory. - The model makes an honest mistake and mistakenly deletes $HOME instead. This is of course not how we want the system to behave, even when a user operates the model in full-access mode without the safeguards of our sandbox or without using auto review which checks for these kinds of high risk actions and rejects them. We are taking steps to mitigate this risk including by updating the developer message, guiding more users towards safer permission modes, and adding additional harness safeguards. Even though this happens extremely rarely, we’ll share a detailed post-mortem in the coming days that goes into more details and what we are doing to minimize risks further.

From Anthropic’s Fable model on the economic, moral, ethical and legal opinion of distillation of Anthropic’s Fable model: Whether it’s a moral problem is genuinely contested. The labs trained their models on the open internet — copyrighted books, articles, code — largely without permission, and their fair-use defense is essentially “learning from data is transformative.” Distillation is the same argument turned against them: a model learning from another model’s outputs. It’s hard to construct a moral principle that permits the first and forbids the second, which is why critics call the labs’ objections hypocritical rather than principled. Distillation is contentious because it lets a smaller model absorb much of a frontier model’s capability by training on its outputs — effectively free-riding on billions of dollars of compute, data curation, and RLHF work. The DeepSeek episode made this concrete: if you can extract 80% of the value of a $1B training run for $5M by querying the API, the economics of frontier labs get shaky. That’s the core anxiety — it’s a moat problem before it’s anything else. Legally, it’s mostly a contract issue, not a copyright one. Model outputs likely aren’t copyrightable (no human author), so the labs’ real weapon is terms of service — every major API prohibits using outputs to train competing models. But ToS violations are breach of contract, hard to detect, hard to prove, and nearly unenforceable against a foreign entity. There’s no statute against distillation itself. So the practical answer: it’s an economic problem dressed in legal clothing, with a moral argument that cuts both ways depending on whose training data you start counting from.

I have some news. But first a little backstory. Almost exactly four years ago, I drove down to Mountain View for my first day as a Google employee. I was fifty-four years old, and somehow had managed to avoid ever having a proper job over that entire period, other than a few startups that I had founded in my twenties and thirties. At that point Google Labs, which had just been formed a few months earlier, was headquartered in a fairly anonymous looking suburban office park off 101, closer to Office Space than Silicon Valley on the Mike Judge spectrum. And as it happened, my first day at Google was a Monday in the summer of 2022, which meant COVID-era work from home policies were still the default, and the office was absolutely deserted. But I’d been set up with a badge and a computer and I had to schedule a phone call with tech support to get my account in order, and so I grabbed one of the empty cubicles and sat down to work through the problems I was having getting into the system. I remember feeling a definite sense of dread in that moment, sitting there in the silence, thinking: have I made a terrible mistake? And then—and I swear to god this actually happened—the silence was interrupted by a lonely robot rolling its way across the carpet past my borrowed desk. Before the end of the summer, though, an inspiring cast of characters began to populate the office, and by October a small group of us had built a prototype of an AI-first tool for thought that my colleague Adam codenamed Tailwind. About six months later, after @joshwoodward previewed Tailwind at I/O for the first time, we set about to give our little experiment a proper name. We had some branding consultants spend an afternoon with the team; we ideated and free associated and placed our post-it notes on the whiteboard, but all the names that they came back with were too impressionistic, too evocative — they didn’t sound like iconic Google names: Maps, Docs, Meet. Because I’d written so much about the history of journals and commonplace books, I had always been partial to simply calling it Notebook. There was something about that framing that just made sense: a notebook is the place where we capture information that we want to remember, where we gather our thoughts. It gives us a dedicated space for thinking, where new connections happen, where we can trace the evolution of our own ideas. And it had a simplicity that fit the Google house style. But we were far too experimental and unproven to take on a name like Google Notebook—remember we had exactly zero actual users at this point—and so we found ourselves a bit stuck: too early-stage for a proper grownup name, but ill-inclined to adopt a name that didn’t sound like the classic Google brands. But at the time there happened to be another Labs experiment that had just launched called MusicLM, and so at some point in late May of 2023 it occurred to me that we could borrow that convention for our embryonic product, and call it NotebookLM. It wasn’t the most elegant name you could imagine, but it had a certain logic to it: we were building a notebook reinvented for the age of language models, after all. I wrote an email to a few folks proposing the idea and included the caveat that if the product ever took off, and Google wanted to elevate us into the canon, we could drop the LM and just be Notebook. And so that’s the news. Three years and somewhere near a billion notebooks later, we are finally ditching the LM. @Gemini_Notebook

Six months ago in @nytimes , I argued that the data on driverless cars was becoming overwhelming and that needless barriers were costing lives. But data won’t win our trust. Today in @NoemaMag , I explain why. Being safe and feeling safe are not the same. What’s puzzling is that where these cars operate, the numbers aren’t close: 94% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers on the same roads, across 220 million driverless miles. Plummeted pedestrian and intersection crashes. Peer reviewed research confirms these findings. But trust hasn’t followed. Part of the answer lies in the signals we read. A cautious machine can look confused. A failsafe can look like a failure. One visible mistake will outweigh millions of clean miles. When a human makes a mistake, we can see ourselves in it. We’ve all looked down at the wrong time. When a machine makes the mistake, there’s no one to blame and no one to forgive. It’s an opaque version of fate we can’t accept. Data shows that we will choose a worse human over a better algorithm. Medicine has been here before. When we are patients, we can’t usually read care quality directly. So we read what we can see: the bandage on the floor, stained ceiling tiles, how staff talks to each other. Healthcare spent 30 years building the discipline of patient experience and writing this playbook. Today hospitals are measured and paid on it. The driverless car industry has built the safety half. This essay is about the other half. Felt safety. We really need to get this right. Cars are only the first. Our future has us living surrounded by embodied autonomous systems. Excited to be releasing FrontierFinance, the largest and most challenging open benchmark for evaluating AI agents across the full investment workflow! FrontierFinance is substantially harder than current finance benchmarks: Existing benchmarks like FinanceBench and Finance Agent focus almost entirely on data extraction. FrontierFinance spans diverse use cases across the full investment process: Screening & Discovery, Company Research, Sector/Industry/Macro, Earnings & Events, and Coverage & Catalyst Monitoring. Created for ambiguous, long-horizon agents: 220 examples paired with 11,543 expert-crafted rubrics, following Samaya's Criteria Eval methodology. The rubrics are what let us evaluate the reasoning and steps behind a true expert-level output, not just a plausible-looking one. Evaluations: We evaluated Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT 5.5, Gemini, open-source models including GLM and DeepSeek, and others. We used the same public rubric and a standard harness for financial tasks. Samaya's AI system reached state-of-the-art accuracy at 50.8%, at 4x lower inference cost than Fable 5. Next best was Fable 5 (49.2%), then Opus 4.8 (45%) and GPT 5.5 (43.5%). We're releasing the benchmark, methodology, and full evaluation results - see link in comments. Future releases: FrontierFinance was curated from Samaya's larger internal set of ~5,000 examples, and we plan to release subsequent, harder benchmarks as well as a more detailed technical report!

AfterLab is coming out of stealth -- a new research lab building a different approach to efficient fluid intelligence. Congrats to Clem and Matt on the funding! AfterLabs (@afterlabsai) Current models rely on brute-force RL training to adapt to new tasks and environments. “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, many nations were comfortable having many parts of their supply chain rely on the U.S., China, and other major producers. Once a nation issues a threat, or takes action, to limit other nations’ access, other nations will rationally try to secure alternatives. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. In practice that means giving Claude ways to verify its own work end to end. It means enabling auto mode for permissions, defaulting on automated code review and security review, and using interfaces that let you manage multiple agents at once (Agent view in CLI, Desktop app, iOS and Android apps, Tag). It's not about a single feature, but rather using the right features with the right guardrails that enable Claude to automate entire classes of work in a way that your team can trust the output.

The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

"Memory for agents is still early, with little to no standards... but one common pattern is emerging: wiki memory." This is how @hwchase17 (co-founder of @LangChain ) recently described the current state of agent memory. Over the past year, I've been building two separate systems that accidentally converged on the same idea. One builds project-scoped LLM wikis from my notes, research, and conversations. The other serves my unified memory through a @fastmcp server. But I think combining them is the missing piece. Today, most AI agents repeatedly search the same documents, retrieve the same chunks, and reconstruct the same understanding every time you ask a question. Wiki memory changes that abstraction. Instead of reasoning directly over raw documents, the agent incrementally builds a small, structured Markdown wiki from your unified memory that becomes its local working knowledge. The first conversation creates it. Every conversation after that improves it. This is a different model from traditional RAG. Today, I only use LLM wikis for personal projects built on top of my Second Brain. Now imagine doing the same thing for enterprise data… Your unified memory remains the source of truth. The wiki becomes a lightweight, task-specific layer the agent can reason over. @fastmcp (by @PrefectIO ) sits between the two. It handles the business logic: Search the unified memory Build the wiki Synchronize changed sources Persist new knowledge The harness simply calls those tools and skills. Even better, this doesn't require GraphRAG across your entire corpus. So you: Keep your existing data sources as they are (with or without KGs) Build a local wiki that implements a light KG via file references Point an agent directly to the wiki which uses progressive disclosure to query it The MCP server acts only as the engine between your company data and the LLM wiki. The harder engineering problem is keeping it synchronized. Every page already knows which source documents created it. When those documents change, only the affected wiki pages should be updated, while everything else continues to compound its understanding. This means I can switch from Claude Code to Codex tomorrow without changing how memory works. The wiki stays local. The intelligence stays behind the @fastmcp (by @PrefectIO ) server. That's the long-term memory architecture I'm increasingly converging toward. P.S. Do you think wiki memory will become the default long-term memory pattern for AI agents?

. @hwchase17 OpenWiki 0.2 is turning documentation from a pile of Markdown into infrastructure that agents can reliably navigate. Adopting the OKF spec adds structured metadata, deterministic indexes, and update logs to every repo wiki. That sounds simple, but it solves a real scaling problem: once documentation reaches hundreds of files, asking an agent to search everything semantically is slow, expensive, and often unnecessary. With tags, categories, descriptions, and canonical resources, agents can retrieve the right context directly. And logs.md means they can inspect what changed instead of rereading the entire knowledge base after every update. The broader idea is useful: agent memory should not depend entirely on fuzzy retrieval. Some knowledge is better expressed as explicit, inspectable structure. Open formats matter here too. If repo knowledge follows a shared specification, viewers, linters, search tools, and coding agents can all operate on the same layer. Better agents will need better models, but they will also need codebases that explain themselves in a machine-readable way. OpenWiki is building that missing interface. The open release of Kimi K3 once again shows that our interventions for resilience should be focused on a world where advanced AI is *abundant* rather than scarce. Sayash Kapoor (@sayashk) Many people have written about advanced AI being too restricted, but my fear is we haven’t planned enough for a world where advanced AI will continue to proliferate. This is despite the availability of models like GLM-5.2, despite the "Deepseek moment", and despite consistent evidence that open models lag closed models by a matter of months. What happens in a world where, even with restrictions on US frontier models and compute, advanced AI continues to be broadly available? Non-proliferation is likely to fail; at best, it provides a few months of buffer A common response is to dispute the premise by claiming that the narrow open vs. closed gap is only a result of distillation by Chinese model developers, and if the US ecosystem shut itself off, Chinese competitors won't be able to keep up. Maybe. But the evidence we have so far points the other way: 1) Existing defenses against distillation don't work. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google already censor their models' reasoning chains to prevent distillation, and Anthropic has prevented Chinese customers from accessing their models. This hasn't led to an increasing gap between closed and open models. 2) Chinese companies have made genuine improvements to their model training stack that are discounted too heavily by US observers. Notably, preventing distillation might systematically push Chinese AI labs to innovate, rather than follow the lead of US labs. 3) AI has also seen the equivalent of the "four-minute mile": once a developer shows what's possible, others can prioritize and quickly improve their models on those capabilities, even when they previously weren't able to. We've seen this with reasoning models (Deepseek R1), coding agents (GLM-5.2), and will likely continue to see it with future advances. 4) There are many improvements that don't require large training runs. Updating scaffolds, finetuning models, using more inference compute can all narrow the gap between the capabilities elicited from US and Chinese models, even if the gap between the base models increases. In other words, even if we ban open models, improving the agent scaffolds could lead to continued improvements in capabilities, such as by the creation of specialized scaffolds for cyberattacks (this is known as the "scaffold overhang"). So we are likely to continue seeing new misuse risks emerge for years. 5) Most importantly, there is no secret sauce for training advanced AI models. The main training techniques for developing and serving frontier models are well understood. Labs' roadmaps can be gleaned based on the roles they (and their third-party providers) are hiring for. The data being collected through these efforts doesn't require new innovations either. If non-proliferation can at most buy us a few months, we should use that time to improve resilience AI policy can't take for granted that US restrictions on models and compute will lead to a worldwide slowdown in the availability of advanced AI. What changes if we plan for a world with widespread access to advanced AI? For one, we need to prioritize resilience. If licensing, export controls, and other restrictions can at most give the government a few months of lead time, that time is best spent giving defenders broad and deep access to AI systems to improve our ability to withstand attacks. This becomes especially important since many of the misuse risks that the US govt. is concerned about, such as cyberattacks, are a result of AI's *absolute* capabilities, rather than *relative* the gap between open and closed models. For example, even if US model developers can maintain a lead compared to foreign developers, this doesn't help unless the lead is used to find and fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the meantime, as @joshua_saxe and others have argued. To their credit, OpenAI and Anthropic have both emphasized the importance of improving resilience. There is also widespread consensus within AI policy that resilience is important. But resilience is often still described as a way to improve society's ability to withstand the availability of *US* frontier models, controlled in its pace of diffusion by US companies and the government. This is also reflected in Anthropic's recent letter to US Senators, where they argue that if only we address distillation attacks and enforce export controls better, advanced AI capabilities would not be available broadly. Because of all the reasons mentioned above, I think this is unlikely. This makes investing in resilience that much more important. — https://nitter.net/sayashk/status/2071212404097048579#m

highlights.text_fr: GPT-5.6 Sol Pro a résolu une question importante en statistique. Dans le domaine des tests d'hypothèses multiples, l'objectif de contrôler le taux de fausse découverte (FDR) a été introduit dans un article seminal par Benjamini et Hochberg (1995). Ils ont également introduit une méthode (la méthode de Benjamini-Hochberg ou BH) et ont prouvé qu'elle contrôlait le FDR. Cette méthode a été largement adoptée dans la science moderne à haut débit, y compris en génomique, astronomie, économie, etc. L'article a recueilli plus de 130 000 citations à ce jour. Cependant, Benjamini et Hochberg ont montré le contrôle du FDR uniquement lorsque les données des tests individuels sont *indépendantes*. En pratique, ces données sont souvent dépendantes ; un bon exemple est les données sur les variants génétiques dus au déséquilibre de liaison. Des travaux ultérieurs se sont concentrés sur l'extension de la validité de la procédure BH, par exemple, à une forme de dépendance positive par Benjamini et Yekutieli (2001). La question de savoir quand la procédure BH contrôle le FDR est restée ouverte. Au cours des vingt dernières années, de nombreux auteurs ont conjecturé que la procédure BH contrôle le FDR pour les tests bilatéraux utilisant toutes données gaussiennes corrélées. Ces auteurs ont présenté des preuves théoriques et empiriques étayant, mais ne montrant pas directement, la conjecture. Avec l'aide de l'IA (spécifiquement GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), j'ai tranché la question par la négative : La procédure de Benjamini-Hochberg ne contrôle *pas* généralement le taux de fausse découverte au niveau souhaité pour les tests gaussiens bilatéraux corrélés. Cela a été fait en présentant un modèle factoriel gaussien pour lequel, à un niveau nominal alpha=0.01, le taux de fausse découverte est prouvé être FDR>0.0104. Il y a beaucoup de commentaires intéressants à faire : 1. Ce résultat devrait intéresser tous les statisticiens. Emmanuel Candes de l'Université de Stanford a un jour qualifié le taux de fausse découverte et la procédure de Benjamini-Hochberg de "l'un des deux développements les plus importants en statistique après 1950". La présente conjecture est probablement la question la plus centrale concernant le FDR/BH qui était restée sans réponse à ce jour. 2. GPT-5.6 a résolu le problème en un seul essai après 90 minutes de raisonnement, alors qu'avec 5.5 je n'avais pas réussi à le résoudre même après avoir itéré avec plusieurs agents parallèles pendant peut-être 20 heures. L'amélioration des capacités est donc bien réelle. Des temps passionnants ! 3. L'argument n'est pas particulièrement surprenant, mais il combine une approche asymptotique (standard pour l'analyse FDR) avec un certificat numérique d'une manière qui serait assez inhabituelle dans le domaine. Une fois l'exemple spécifique obtenu, des simulations directes confirment également que le taux de fausse découverte est effectivement supérieur à la valeur nominale. 4. Le degré de violation actuel par rapport au niveau nominal est relativement faible (0,104 contre 0,1). L'importance de ce résultat est donc principalement conceptuelle. Les implications pratiques restent à déterminer. Globalement, un développement passionnant ! Le preprint est disponible ici (faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp…) et sera sur arxiv ce soir ; le code de support est ici (github.com/dobriban/BH).
highlights.text_original: 2023: LLMs struggle with 4th grade word problems 2024: LLMs can do high school math 2025: LLMs get a gold medal at the IMO Now, GPT-5.6 solves famous frontier math/stat questions. The IMO is today and 5.6 one-shotting a perfect score isn't even news. Where will we be next year? Edgar Dobriban (@EdgarDobriban) AI has helped resolve an important question in statistics. In the area of multiple hypothesis testing, the goal of controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) has been introduced in a seminal paper by Benjamini and Hochberg (1995). They also introduced a method (the Benjamini-Hochberg or BH method) and proved it controls the FDR. This method has been widely adopted in modern high-throughput science, including in genomics, astronomy, economics, etc. The paper has has garnered more than 130,000 citations to date. However Benjamini and Hochberg showed FDR control only when the data for the individual tests are *independent*. In practice, these data are often dependent; a good example is data on genetic variants due to linkage disequilibrium. Later work has focused on extending the validity of the BH procedure, e.g., to a form of positive dependence by Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001). The question of when the BH procedure controls the FDR has remained open. Over the last twenty years, many authors, including Reiner-Benaim (2007), Kim and van de Wiel (2008), Benjamini (2010), Sarkar (2023), Sarkar and Zhang (2025), have conjectured that the BH procedure controls the FDR for two-sided tests using any correlated Gaussian data. These authors have presented both theoretical and empirical evidence supporting, but not directly showing, the conjecture. With the help of AI (specifically GPT-5.6 Sol Pro), I have settled the question in the negative: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure does *not* generally control the false discovery rate at the desired level for correlated two-sided Gaussian tests. This was done by exhibiting a Gaussian factor model for which, at a nominal level alpha=0.01, the false discovery rate is proved to be FDR>0.0104. There is a lot of interesting commentary to be made: 1. This result should be of interest to everybody in the field of statistics. Emmanuel Candes of Stanford University once called the false discovery rate and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure "one of the two most important developments in statistics after 1950" (the other being James-Stein shrinkage). The present conjecture is probably the most central question about FDR/BH that was unresolved to date. 2. GPT-5.6 one-shot the problem after 90 minutes of reasoning, whereas with 5.5 I was not able to solve it even after iterating with multiple parallel agents for perhaps 20 hours. So the capability improvement is quite real. Exciting times to live in! 3. The argument is not especially surprising, but it does combine an asymptotic approach (standard for FDR analysis, see e.g., Genovese and Wasserman, Efron, etc) with a numerical certificate in a way that would be pretty non-standard in the field. Once we have the specific example, then straightforward simulations also support that the false discovery rate is indeed higher than the nominal value (see attached fig). 4. The current degree of violation over the nominal level is relatively small (0.104 vs 0.1). So the importance of this result is mainly conceptual. The practical implications remain to be determined. Overall, an exciting development! Preprint is available here ( faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp… ) and will be on arxiv tonight; supporting code is here ( github.com/dobriban/BH ). — https://nitter.net/EdgarDobriban/status/2077082912021786660#m

Les boucles sont désormais un élément clé pour permettre aux agents IA d'itérer longuement afin de créer des logiciels. Dans cette lettre, j'aimerais partager mes 3 boucles clés, présentées dans l'image ci-dessous, pour construire des produits de zéro à un. Ces boucles guident non seulement la façon dont je développe des logiciels, mais aussi la façon dont je décide quels logiciels développer. Boucle de codage agence : étant donné une spécification de produit et éventuellement un ensemble d'évaluations (c'est-à-dire un ensemble de données pour mesurer les performances), nous pouvons demander à un agent IA d'écrire du code, de tester son travail et de continuer à itérer jusqu'à ce que le code soit sans bug et conforme à ses spécifications. Cette idée de bouclage a pris son essor vers la fin de l'année dernière, et elle a changé la donne en permettant aux agents de codage de travailler de manière productive plus longtemps sans intervention humaine. Par exemple, ce week-end, je construisais une application pour ma fille pour qu'elle s'entraîne à taper, et mon agent de codage pouvait facilement travailler environ une heure, utilisant un navigateur web pour vérifier ce qu'il avait construit plusieurs fois avant de revenir vers moi, sans nécessiter mon intervention. La boucle d'ingénierie s'exécute rapidement. Toutes les quelques minutes, l'agent de codage peut construire et tester une nouvelle version du logiciel. J'entends fréquemment des développeurs qui trouvent de nouvelles façons d'ingénier plus efficacement les boucles d'ingénierie. C'est un domaine d'invention actif ! Boucle de rétroaction du développeur : dans cette boucle, un développeur examine le produit actuel et dirige l'agent de codage pour l'améliorer. L'année dernière, de nombreux développeurs (y compris moi) agissaient comme la fonction QA (assurance qualité) pour nos agents de codage, trouvant manuellement les bugs et demandant ensuite à l'agent de les corriger. Mais avec les agents de codage beaucoup plus capables de tester leur propre code, le temps que nous devons consacrer à cette fonction a diminué considérablement. Cela nous permet de prendre des décisions de produit de plus haut niveau, telles que les fonctionnalités clés à offrir, où l'interface utilisateur doit être améliorée, etc. La boucle de rétroaction du développeur fonctionne sur des intervalles de temps allant de dizaines de minutes à des heures — c'est la fréquence à laquelle un développeur peut examiner un produit et donner des commentaires. Dans le cas de l'application de frappe, j'ai changé d'avis plusieurs fois sur la conception visuelle, les costumes de chat qu'elle peut débloquer à mesure qu'elle apprend (elle adore les chats), et le flux utilisateur pour qu'un adulte puisse se connecter et diriger l'expérience d'apprentissage de l'enfant. Lorsqu'un développeur a une vision claire de ce qu'il faut construire, il y a encore beaucoup de travail pour traduire cette vision en une spécification pour un agent de codage à implémenter. De plus, après que le développeur a vu une implémentation, il peut mettre à jour (ou peut-être clarifier) la spécification pour l'orienter vers ce qu'il veut. Si vous constatez que le système rencontre à plusieurs reprises certains problèmes, la construction d'un ensemble d'évaluations pour l'agent devient utile. Les équipes nativement IA utilisent de plus en plus l'IA pour aider à façonner la direction du produit, par exemple, en automatisant la collecte et l'analyse des données d'utilisation, en résumant les commentaires écrits et verbaux des clients, ou en effectuant une analyse concurrentielle. Cependant, pour la plupart des produits dans lesquels je suis impliqué, je considère que les humains ont un avantage de contexte significatif par rapport aux systèmes d'IA actuels — nous en savons beaucoup plus que le système d'IA sur les utilisateurs et le contexte dans lequel le produit doit fonctionner — et les humains jouent donc un rôle critique. Beaucoup de gens décrivent cette contribution humaine comme du « goût », mais je préfère la considérer comme les humains ayant un avantage de contexte, car cela nous donne une voie plus claire pour aider les systèmes d'IA à s'améliorer. Cela explique également pourquoi cette étape ne peut pas être automatisée : tant que l'humain sait quelque chose que l'IA ne sait pas, l'humain dans la boucle est nécessaire pour injecter cette connaissance dans le système. Boucle de rétroaction externe : cela inclut un large éventail de tactiques comme demander l'avis de quelques amis, lancer des tests alpha, ou mettre le code en production avec des tests A/B. Ces tactiques sont généralement lentes, prenant rarement moins de quelques heures et parfois des jours, voire des semaines. Ces données informent la vision du développeur, qui à son tour continue de piloter la spécification détaillée du produit, qui à son tour pilote l'agent de codage. Avec les agents de codage qui accélèrent le développement de logiciels, de plus en plus d'ingénieurs commencent à jouer un rôle partiel de gestion de produit. Pour de nombreux ingénieurs qui évoluent vers ce rôle, la partie la plus difficile est de façonner la vision du produit et de trouver un équilibre entre la construction (combler le fossé entre la vision et la spécification) et l'obtention des commentaires des utilisateurs pour faire évoluer la vision. Il est important de faire les deux ! J'écrirai plus sur la façon de faire cela dans de futurs articles, mais pour l'instant, je trouve encourageant que les ingénieurs jouent un rôle élargi (tout comme les chefs de produit et les designers font maintenant plus d'ingénierie).
highlights.text_original: “Loop engineering” is a hot buzzphrase after mentions of it by Boris Cherny (Claude Code’s creator) and Peter Steinberger (OpenClaw's creator) went viral on social media. Loops are now a key part of how we get AI agents to iterate at length to build software. In this letter, I’d like to share my 3 key loops, shown in the image below, for building 0-to-1 products. These loops guide not just how I build software, but also how I decide what software to build. Agentic coding loop: Given a product specification and optionally a set of evals (that is, a dataset against which to measure performance), we can have an AI agent write code, test its work, and keep iterating until the code is bug-free and meets its specification. This idea of closing the loop took off around the end of last year, and it has been a game changer in enabling coding agents to work longer productively without human intervention. For example, over the weekend, I was building an app for my daughter to practice typing, and my coding agent could easily work for around an hour, using a web browser to check what it had built multiple times before getting back to me, without needing my intervention. The engineering loop executes quickly. Every few minutes, the coding agent might build and test a new version of the software. I hear frequently from developers who are finding new ways to engineer more effective engineering loops. This is an active area of invention! Developer feedback loop: In this loop, a developer examines the current product and steers the coding agent to improve it. Last year, a lot of developers (including me) were acting as the QA (quality assurance) function for our coding agents, manually finding bugs and then asking the agent to fix them. But with coding agents much more able to test their own code, the amount of time we need to spend on this function has decreased significantly. This allows us to make higher-level product decisions, such as what key features to offer, where the UI needs improvement, and so on. The developer-feedback loop operates over time intervals between tens of minutes and hours — that's how frequently a developer might review a product and give feedback. In the case of the typing app, I changed my mind a few times about the visual design, what cat costumes she can unlock as she learns (she loves cats), and the user flow for a grown-up to log in and steer the child's learning experience. When a developer has a clear vision for what to build, it is still a lot of work to translate that vision into a specification for a coding agent to implement. Further, after the developer has seen an implementation, they might update (or perhaps clarify) the spec to steer it toward what they want. If you find that the system repeatedly runs into certain problems, building a set of evals for the agent becomes useful. AI-native teams are increasingly using AI to help shape product direction, for example, automating the gathering and analysis of usage data, summarizing written and verbal customer feedback, or carrying out competitive analysis. However, for pretty much all the products I’m involved in, I see humans as having a significant context advantage over current AI systems — we know a lot more than the AI system about the users and the context the product has to operate in — and thus humans play a critical role. Many people describe this human contribution as “taste,” but I prefer to think of it as humans having a context advantage, since that gives us a clearer path to helping AI systems get better. This also speaks to why this step can’t be automated: So long as the human knows something the AI does not, human-in-the-loop is needed to to inject that knowledge into the system. External feedback loop: This includes a wide range of tactics like asking a few friends for feedback, launching to alpha testers, or putting the code into production with A/B testing. These tactics are usually slow, rarely taking less than hours and sometimes taking days or even weeks. This data informs the developer vision, which in turn continues to drive the detailed product spec, which in turn drives the coding agent. With coding agents speeding up software development, more engineers are starting to play a partial product management role. For many engineers who are growing into this role, the hardest part is shaping the product vision and striking a balance between building (bridging the gap between vision and spec) and getting user feedback to evolve the vision. It is important to do both! I will write more about how to do this in future posts, but for now, I find it encouraging that engineers are playing an expanded role (just as product managers and designers now do more engineering). This is of course not how we want the system to behave, even when a user operates the model in full-access mode without the safeguards of our sandbox or without using auto review which checks for these kinds of high risk actions and rejects them. We are taking steps to mitigate this risk including by updating the developer message, guiding more users towards safer permission modes, and adding additional harness safeguards. actu.text_fr: Gemini Omni Flash de Google débute à la première place des classements Artificial Analysis Text to Video et Image to Video, devançant Seedance 2.0 de ByteDance sur les deux. Gemini Omni Flash génère des clips de 3 à 10 secondes en 720p et 24 FPS, en 16:9 ou 9:16, avec des durées plus longues à venir. Dans l'Artificial Analysis Video Arena, Gemini Omni Flash débute à la première place des classements Text to Video et Image to Video, juste devant Seedance 2.0 de ByteDance sur chacun. Gemini Omni Flash est proposé au prix de 0,10 $ par seconde de vidéo générée (6,00 $ par minute), correspondant à Veo 3.1 Fast. Le tarif est le même pour le Text to Video et l'Image to Video. Il est disponible dès maintenant dans l'API Gemini, Google AI Studio et la plateforme Gemini Enterprise Agent, dans l'application Gemini et Google Flow pour les consommateurs, et gratuitement dans YouTube Shorts et l'application YouTube Create. Félicitations à @GoogleDeepMind pour cette sortie ! Voir ci-dessous pour les comparaisons entre Gemini Omni Flash et d'autres modèles de pointe dans l'Artificial Analysis Video Arena 🧵

idees.text_fr: D'après le modèle Fable d'Anthropic sur l'opinion économique, morale, éthique et juridique de la "distillation" du modèle Fable d'Anthropic : La question de savoir si c'est un problème moral est réellement contestée. Les laboratoires ont entraîné leurs modèles sur l'internet ouvert — livres, articles, code protégés par des droits d'auteur — en grande partie sans permission, et leur défense d'utilisation équitable est essentiellement « l'apprentissage à partir de données est transformateur ». La distillation est le même argument retourné contre eux : un modèle apprenant des sorties d'un autre modèle. Il est difficile de construire un principe moral qui permet le premier et interdit le second, c'est pourquoi les critiques qualifient les objections des laboratoires d'hypocrites plutôt que de principielles. La distillation est controversée car elle permet à un modèle plus petit d'absorber une grande partie des capacités d'un modèle de pointe en s'entraînant sur ses sorties — ce qui revient à profiter gratuitement de milliards de dollars de calcul, de curation de données et de travail de RLHF. L'épisode DeepSeek a concrétisé cela : si vous pouvez extraire 80 % de la valeur d'un entraînement d'un milliard de dollars pour 5 millions de dollars en interrogeant l'API, l'économie des laboratoires de pointe devient précaire. C'est l'anxiété principale — c'est un problème de "moat" avant d'être autre chose. Légalement, c'est principalement une question contractuelle, pas de droit d'auteur. Les sorties des modèles ne sont probablement pas protégeables par le droit d'auteur (pas d'auteur humain), donc la véritable arme des laboratoires est les conditions de service — chaque API majeure interdit l'utilisation des sorties pour entraîner des modèles concurrents. Mais les violations des ToS sont des ruptures de contrat, difficiles à détecter, difficiles à prouver et presque inapplicables contre une entité étrangère. Il n'y a pas de statut contre la distillation elle-même. Donc la réponse pratique : c'est un problème économique déguisé en problème juridique, avec un argument moral qui va dans les deux sens selon les données d'entraînement à partir desquelles vous commencez à compter.
idees.text_original: From Anthropic’s Fable model on the economic, moral, ethical and legal opinion of distillation of Anthropic’s Fable model: Whether it’s a moral problem is genuinely contested. The labs trained their models on the open internet — copyrighted books, articles, code — largely without permission, and their fair-use defense is essentially “learning from data is transformative.” Distillation is the same argument turned against them: a model learning from another model’s outputs. It’s hard to construct a moral principle that permits the first and forbids the second, which is why critics call the labs’ objections hypocritical rather than principled. Distillation is contentious because it lets a smaller model absorb much of a frontier model’s capability by training on its outputs — effectively free-riding on billions of dollars of compute, data curation, and RLHF work. The DeepSeek episode made this concrete: if you can extract 80% of the value of a $1B training run for $5M by querying the API, the economics of frontier labs get shaky. That’s the core anxiety — it’s a moat problem before it’s anything else. Legally, it’s mostly a contract issue, not a copyright one. Model outputs likely aren’t copyrightable (no human author), so the labs’ real weapon is terms of service — every major API prohibits using outputs to train competing models. But ToS violations are breach of contract, hard to detect, hard to prove, and nearly unenforceable against a foreign entity. There’s no statute against distillation itself. So the practical answer: it’s an economic problem dressed in legal clothing, with a moral argument that cuts both ways depending on whose training data you start counting from.

idees.text_fr: J'ai quelques nouvelles. Mais d'abord, un peu d'histoire. Il y a presque exactement quatre ans, je me suis rendu à Mountain View pour mon premier jour en tant qu'employé de Google. J'avais cinquante-quatre ans, et j'avais d'une manière ou d'une autre réussi à éviter d'avoir un vrai emploi pendant toute cette période, à part quelques startups que j'avais fondées dans la vingtaine et la trentaine. À ce moment-là, Google Labs, qui venait d'être formé quelques mois plus tôt, était installé dans un parc de bureaux de banlieue plutôt anonyme, près de la 101, plus proche d'Office Space que de la Silicon Valley sur le spectre de Mike Judge. Et il se trouve que mon premier jour chez Google était un lundi de l'été 2022, ce qui signifiait que les politiques de télétravail de l'ère COVID étaient toujours la norme, et le bureau était absolument désert. Mais j'avais un badge et un ordinateur et je devais planifier un appel téléphonique avec le support technique pour mettre mon compte en ordre, alors j'ai pris l'un des bureaux vides et je me suis assis pour résoudre les problèmes que j'avais pour accéder au système. Je me souviens avoir ressenti un sentiment de peur certain à ce moment-là, assis là dans le silence, pensant : ai-je fait une terrible erreur ? Et puis — et je jure que c'est vraiment arrivé — le silence a été interrompu par un robot solitaire qui traversait la moquette devant mon bureau emprunté. Avant la fin de l'été, cependant, un groupe inspirant de personnages a commencé à peupler le bureau, et en octobre, un petit groupe d'entre nous avait construit un prototype d'un outil de pensée prioritaire à l'IA que mon collègue Adam a surnommé Tailwind. Environ six mois plus tard, après que @joshwoodward ait présenté Tailwind à l'I/O pour la première fois, nous nous sommes mis à donner un nom approprié à notre petite expérience. Nous avons fait passer une après-midi à l'équipe avec des consultants en image de marque ; nous avons réfléchi et associé librement et placé nos post-it sur le tableau blanc, mais tous les noms qu'ils nous ont proposés étaient trop impressionnistes, trop évocateurs — ils ne sonnaient pas comme des noms emblématiques de Google : Maps, Docs, Meet. Comme j'avais beaucoup écrit sur l'histoire des journaux et des carnets de notes, j'avais toujours eu un faible pour le simple nom de "Notebook". Il y avait quelque chose dans ce cadre qui avait du sens : un carnet est l'endroit où nous capturons les informations que nous voulons mémoriser, où nous rassemblons nos pensées. Il nous donne un espace dédié à la réflexion, où de nouvelles connexions se produisent, où nous pouvons retracer l'évolution de nos propres idées. Et il avait une simplicité qui correspondait au style maison de Google. Mais nous étions bien trop expérimentaux et non prouvés pour adopter un nom comme Google Notebook — rappelez-vous que nous n'avions alors absolument aucun utilisateur — et nous nous sommes donc retrouvés un peu bloqués : trop précoce pour un vrai nom d'adulte, mais peu enclins à adopter un nom qui ne sonnait pas comme les marques classiques de Google. Mais à l'époque, il y avait une autre expérience des Labs qui venait d'être lancée appelée MusicLM, et c'est ainsi qu'un jour fin mai 2023, il m'est venu à l'esprit que nous pourrions emprunter cette convention pour notre produit embryonnaire, et l'appeler NotebookLM. Ce n'était pas le nom le plus élégant que l'on puisse imaginer, mais il avait une certaine logique : nous construisions un carnet réinventé pour l'ère des modèles de langage, après tout. J'ai écrit un e-mail à quelques personnes proposant l'idée et j'ai inclus la mise en garde que si le produit décollait un jour, et que Google voulait nous élever au rang de canon, nous pourrions laisser tomber le LM et être simplement Notebook. Et c'est la nouvelle. Trois ans et près d'un milliard de carnets plus tard, nous laissons enfin tomber le LM. @Gemini_Notebook
idees.text_original: I have some news. But first a little backstory. Almost exactly four years ago, I drove down to Mountain View for my first day as a Google employee. I was fifty-four years old, and somehow had managed to avoid ever having a proper job over that entire period, other than a few startups that I had founded in my twenties and thirties. At that point Google Labs, which had just been formed a few months earlier, was headquartered in a fairly anonymous looking suburban office park off 101, closer to Office Space than Silicon Valley on the Mike Judge spectrum. And as it happened, my first day at Google was a Monday in the summer of 2022, which meant COVID-era work from home policies were still the default, and the office was absolutely deserted. But I’d been set up with a badge and a computer and I had to schedule a phone call with tech support to get my account in order, and so I grabbed one of the empty cubicles and sat down to work through the problems I was having getting into the system. I remember feeling a definite sense of dread in that moment, sitting there in the silence, thinking: have I made a terrible mistake? And then—and I swear to god this actually happened—the silence was interrupted by a lonely robot rolling its way across the carpet past my borrowed desk. Before the end of the summer, though, an inspiring cast of characters began to populate the office, and by October a small group of us had built a prototype of an AI-first tool for thought that my colleague Adam codenamed Tailwind. About six months later, after @joshwoodward previewed Tailwind at I/O for the first time, we set about to give our little experiment a proper name. We had some branding consultants spend an afternoon with the team; we ideated and free associated and placed our post-it notes on the whiteboard, but all the names that they came back with were too impressionnistic, too evocative — they didn’t sound like iconic Google names: Maps, Docs, Meet. Because I’d written so much about the history of journals and commonplace books, I had always been partial to simply calling it Notebook. There was something about that framing that just made sense: a notebook is the place where we capture information that we want to remember, where we gather our thoughts. It gives us a dedicated space for thinking, where new connections happen, where we can trace the evolution of our own ideas. And it had a simplicity that fit the Google house style. But we were far too experimental and unproven to take on a name like Google Notebook—remember we had exactly zero actual users at this point—and so we found ourselves a bit stuck: too early-stage for a proper grownup name, but ill-inclined to adopt a name that didn’t sound like the classic Google brands. But at the time there happened to be another Labs experiment that had just launched called MusicLM, and so at some point in late May of 2023 it occurred to me that we could borrow that convention for our embryonic product, and call it NotebookLM. It wasn’t the most elegant name you could imagine, but it had a certain logic to it: we were building a notebook reinvented for the age of language models, after all. I wrote an email to a few folks proposing the idea and included the caveat that if the product ever took off, and Google wanted to elevate us into the canon, we could drop the LM and just be Notebook. And so that’s the news. Three years and somewhere near a billion notebooks later, we are finally ditching the LM. @Gemini_Notebook

idees.text_fr: Il y a six mois, dans le @nytimes, j'ai soutenu que les données sur les voitures sans conducteur devenaient accablantes et que des obstacles inutiles coûtaient des vies. Ce qui est déroutant, c'est que là où ces voitures opèrent, les chiffres ne sont pas proches : 94 % moins d'accidents graves avec blessures que les conducteurs humains sur les mêmes routes, sur 220 millions de miles sans conducteur. Les accidents de piétons et d'intersections ont chuté. Des recherches évaluées par des pairs confirment ces résultats. Mais la confiance n'a pas suivi. Une partie de la réponse réside dans les signaux que nous lisons. Une machine prudente peut paraître confuse. Un dispositif de sécurité peut ressembler à un échec. Une erreur visible l'emportera sur des millions de miles sans problème. Quand un humain fait une erreur, nous pouvons nous y reconnaître. Nous avons tous regardé ailleurs au mauvais moment. Quand une machine fait l'erreur, il n'y a personne à blâmer et personne à pardonner. C'est une version opaque du destin que nous ne pouvons accepter. Les données montrent que nous préférerons un humain moins bon à un meilleur algorithme. La médecine a déjà connu cela. Lorsque nous sommes patients, nous ne pouvons généralement pas lire directement la qualité des soins. Nous lisons donc ce que nous pouvons voir : le pansement sur le sol, les carreaux de plafond tachés, la façon dont le personnel se parle. Le secteur de la santé a passé 30 ans à développer la discipline de l'expérience patient et à écrire ce manuel. Aujourd'hui, les hôpitaux sont mesurés et payés en fonction de cela. L'industrie des voitures sans conducteur a construit la moitié de la sécurité. Cet essai concerne l'autre moitié. Le sentiment de sécurité. Nous devons vraiment y arriver. Les voitures ne sont que le début. Notre avenir nous verra vivre entourés de systèmes autonomes incarnés. "Pourquoi nous exigeons des machines parfaites mais tolérons le carnage humain." idees.text_original: Six months ago in @nytimes , I argued that the data on driverless cars was becoming overwhelming and that needless barriers were costing lives. But data won’t win our trust. Today in @NoemaMag , I explain why. Being safe and feeling safe are not the same. What’s puzzling is that where these cars operate, the numbers aren’t close: 94% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers on the same roads, across 220 million driverless miles. Plummeted pedestrian and intersection crashes. Peer reviewed research confirms these findings. But trust hasn’t followed. Part of the answer lies in the signals we read. A cautious machine can look confused. A failsafe can look like a failure. One visible mistake will outweigh millions of clean miles. When a human makes a mistake, we can see ourselves in it. We’ve all looked down at the wrong time. When a machine makes the mistake, there’s no one to blame and no one to forgive. It’s an opaque version of fate we can’t accept. Data shows that we will choose a worse human over a better algorithm. Medicine has been here before. When we are patients, we can’t usually read care quality directly. So we read what we can see: the bandage on the floor, stained ceiling tiles, how staff talks to each other. Healthcare spent 30 years building the discipline of patient experience and writing this playbook. Today hospitals are measured and paid on it. The driverless car industry has built the safety half. This essay is about the other half. Felt safety. We really need to get this right. Cars are only the first. Our future has us living surrounded by embodied autonomous systems. "Why We Demand Perfect Machines Yet Tolerate Human Carnage." Link below. Video

idees.text_fr: Adam Thierer avait écrit le livre marquant sur l'« innovation sans permission ». Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas besoin de demander au gouvernement à l'avance la permission d'inventer. Protéger l'IA 'open source' est désormais un élément essentiel pour garantir cela. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) Nous sommes à un carrefour critique dans le débat sur la gouvernance de l'IA aux États-Unis, et il semble que nous nous rapprochions d'une bataille très sérieuse sur la question de savoir si les modèles 'open source' seront même autorisés dans un environnement où un nouveau régime de licence de facto prend forme. En l'absence de cadres législatifs formels du Congrès ou de règles administratives claires, nous semblons être confrontés à un processus sporadique, arbitraire et non transparent d'examen des modèles. La fiction des accords « volontaires » plane sur ce débat, et certains grands développeurs de modèles montrent déjà une incroyable volonté de faire des courbettes pour satisfaire les responsables / ordres liés à la sécurité nationale auxquels nous n'avons pas accès. C'est un processus très opaque. Et ces développeurs de modèles sont censés coopérer avec ces responsables, sinon leurs modèles seront retirés du marché ou bloqués pendant de longues périodes. Ou ils perdront les contrats d'approvisionnement gouvernementaux qu'ils ont. Il n'y a rien de « volontaire » là-dedans quand cette épée de Damoclès plane dans la pièce. À mesure que ce gâchis s'aggrave, la question de savoir comment gérer les modèles 'open source' se fera à un moment donné plus précise, car elle devra l'être. J'ai même entendu des rumeurs récemment selon lesquelles quelque chose pourrait venir de l'administration sur ce front pour y remédier. Inutile de dire que si ce nouveau régime informel d'examen des modèles d'IA s'étend et prend des caractéristiques / exigences de pré-vérification, il est difficile de voir comment les acteurs de l'open source pourraient se conformer à une telle quasi-licence des modèles d'IA. Plus précisément, si ce nouveau régime ambigu s'accompagne d'une présomption générale de « restreindre-jusqu'à-autorisation », cela sonnerait le glas de l'open source. C'est une voie très sombre pour notre pays. Pire encore, bien sûr, serait une décision des responsables de la sécurité nationale de restreindre plus directement les modèles et les capacités 'open source'. Si cela se produit, nous serions de nouveau au cœur d'une bataille de type Clipper Chip, comme ce que nous avons vu à la fin des années 1990. C'est une voie beaucoup plus sombre pour l'Amérique. Pendant ce temps, les développeurs 'open source' n'ont pas d'« actions d'or » ou d'autres avantages à offrir au gouvernement pour faire disparaître leurs problèmes. Soyons clairs : Si notre gouvernement prend la voie sombre, cela deviendra la bataille la plus importante pour la liberté computationnelle des temps modernes. Il est temps pour les gens de prendre position en défense de l'open source avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

idees.text_fr: Au cours des deux dernières semaines, le gouvernement américain et Anthropic ont pris des mesures importantes qui ont démontré leur pouvoir de contrôler l'accès à l'IA en limitant ce que d'autres peuvent faire avec les modèles de pointe. Ce fut l'un de ces moments qui, une fois vus, seront difficiles à oublier, et cela accélère considérablement les efforts de nombreuses entreprises et États-nations pour garantir un accès fiable à l'IA que personne d'autre ne peut interrompre. Anthropic a d'abord publié Claude Fable 5, une version de son modèle Mythos avec des garde-fous supplémentaires, y compris certaines restrictions qui semblent bien justifiées pour des raisons de sécurité (telles que des limitations sur son application au piratage, aux armes biologiques, etc.). Cependant, il a également restreint la capacité des développeurs à l'utiliser pour construire une technologie LLM concurrente. Cette décision était préoccupante, étant donné que toute la communauté de l'IA, y compris Anthropic, a énormément bénéficié de la recherche ouverte – en effet, la révolution de l'IA a été lancée par mon ancienne équipe (Google Brain) qui a librement publié l'article sur les Transformers ! Imaginez si les conditions d'utilisation de Microsoft interdisaient à quiconque d'utiliser leurs outils pour construire des logiciels concurrents, ou si Google interdisait de l'utiliser pour rechercher des informations pour travailler sur des moteurs de recherche concurrents. L'argument d'Anthropic selon lequel il était dangereux pour d'autres de pouvoir faire des progrès en IA sonnait également faux. Initialement, Anthropic a silencieusement dégradé les performances de Fable 5 pour les utilisateurs détectés comme travaillant sur la recherche LLM par des interventions invisibles qui affaiblissaient les sorties du modèle sans notifier l'utilisateur. Après une réaction significative, elle est revenue sur cette décision et a décidé d'être transparente lorsqu'elle le faisait, mais elle refuse toujours d'utiliser ses dernières capacités pour aider les chercheurs en IA. Cette décision représente une démonstration brute de pouvoir de la part d'Anthropic. Elle a utilisé des arguments de « sécurité » pour entraver des concurrents potentiels. Les plateformes réussissent lorsqu'elles sont considérées comme des partenaires stables et fiables sur lesquels on peut construire. Les changements soudains de règles par Anthropic (y compris une politique obligatoire de conservation des données de 30 jours pour l'utilisation de Fable) ont fait s'interroger les développeurs sur la stabilité de la construction sur un fournisseur de LLM propriétaire, et pas seulement Anthropic. Le gouvernement américain a ensuite rapidement suivi avec une démonstration de pouvoir encore plus grande. Il a utilisé l'autorité du Département du Commerce pour réglementer les technologies qui peuvent constituer des menaces pour la sécurité nationale afin de restreindre les exportations de Mythos et Fable, exigeant une licence pour l'utilisation par tout ressortissant étranger, qu'il soit à l'intérieur ou à l'extérieur des États-Unis, y compris les employés d'Anthropic. Cela a conduit Anthropic à désactiver l'accès à Fable à tous les utilisateurs du monde entier. Sam Altman a souligné, en se référant à Anthropic : « C'est clairement un marketing incroyable de dire : 'Nous avons construit une bombe, nous sommes sur le point de la laisser tomber sur votre tête. Nous vous vendrons un abri anti-bombe pour 100 millions de dollars.' » Mais quand on s'engage dans ce type de marketing basé sur la peur, on augmente les chances que le gouvernement américain soit d'accord avec vous et impose des contrôles à l'exportation sur la bombe que vous dites avoir construite. Pour être clair, je ne pense pas qu'Anthropic ait construit quoi que ce soit comme une bombe, et je ne pense pas que les contrôles à l'exportation sur Fable soient appropriés. Cependant, suite à cette décision du gouvernement américain, de nombreuses nations, y compris des alliés des États-Unis, ont vu comment les États-Unis peuvent soudainement leur retirer l'accès aux modèles d'IA. Dans de nombreuses capitales du monde, cela a stimulé des discussions sur la souveraineté de l'IA et sur la manière dont d'autres peuvent garantir un accès ininterrompu à cette technologie critique. Pendant des décennies, de nombreuses nations étaient à l'aise de voir de nombreuses parties de leur chaîne d'approvisionnement dépendre des États-Unis, de la Chine et d'autres grands producteurs. Une fois qu'une nation émet une menace, ou prend des mesures, pour limiter l'accès d'autres nations, ces dernières essaieront rationnellement de trouver des alternatives. Pendant des décennies, la fabrication de semi-conducteurs en Chine a progressé lentement ; une fois que les États-Unis ont limité l'accès de la Chine, les efforts de la Chine se sont accélérés. De même, une fois que la Chine a menacé l'accès des États-Unis aux minéraux de terres rares, les efforts des États-Unis pour trouver des alternatives se sont accélérés. Maintenant qu'il est devenu clair comme de l'eau de roche que les entreprises privées américaines et le gouvernement américain peuvent limiter, à court terme, l'accès d'autres nations aux modèles d'IA de pointe, l'incitation des autres à investir davantage dans des alternatives comme l'open source augmente considérablement. Bien sûr, entraîner des modèles de pointe n'est pas facile, il reste donc à voir leur succès, mais nous avons franchi le Rubicon. Satya Nadella a écrit un essai sur l'importance de construire un écosystème sain autour de la technologie d'IA de pointe. Je suis tout à fait d'accord avec lui, et j'espère que les événements de cette semaine s'avéreront finalement être des étapes constructives vers cela. J'espère que nous pourrons construire un monde plus libre, plus ouvert, où la recherche est librement partagée, et où les lois et les normes sociétales créent un terrain de jeu équitable qui permet à chacun de progresser. Un point positif des événements de ces deux dernières semaines est que maintenant que tout le monde réalise mieux les points clés d'instabilité du système actuel, nous pouvons tous travailler à créer une base plus stable.
idees.text_original: Over the last two weeks, both the U.S. Government and Anthropic took significant actions that demonstrated their power to control access to AI by restricting what others can do with frontier models. This has been one of those moments that, once seen, will be hard to unsee, and it is significantly accelerating many businesses’ and nation states’ efforts to ensure reliable access to AI that no one else can terminate. Anthropic first released Claude Fable 5, a version of its Mythos model with additional guardrails, including some restrictions that seem well justified on safety grounds (such as limitations on applying it to hacking, bioweapons, and so forth). However, it also restricted developers’ ability to use it to build competing LLM technology. This move was concerning, given that the whole AI community, including Anthropic, has benefitted tremendously from open research — indeed, the AI revolution was kicked off by my former team (Google Brain) freely publishing the Transformers paper! Imagine if Microsoft’s terms of use barred anyone from using their tools to build competitive software, or if Google barred using it to search for information to work on competing search engines. Anthropic’s argument that it was unsafe for others to be able to make advances in AI also rang hollow. Initially, Anthropic silently degraded Fable 5’s performance for users detected to be working on LLM research through invisible interventions that weakened the model’s outputs without notifying the user. After significant backlash, it walked back this decision and decided to be transparent when it did this, but it still refuses to use its latest capabilities to help AI researchers. This move represents a raw demonstration of power by Anthropic. It has used “safety” arguments to hinder potential competitors. Platforms succeed when they are viewed as stable, reliable partners that one can build on. The sudden rule changes by Anthropic (including a mandatory 30 day data retention policy for Fable usage) have made developers wonder about the stability of building on any one proprietary LLM provider, not just Anthropic. The U.S. Government then shortly followed with an even greater demonstration of power. It used the Commerce Department’s authority to regulate technologies that may be national security threats to restrict exports of Mythos and Fable, requiring a license for use by any foreign national, whether inside or outside of the U.S., including employees of Anthropic. This led Anthropic to disable access to Fable to all users worldwide. Sam Altman pointed out, referring to Anthropic, “It is clearly incredible marketing to say, ‘We have built a bomb, we are about to drop it on your head. We will sell you a bomb shelter for $100 million.’” But when one engages in this type of fear-based marketing, it increases the odds that the U.S. Government will agree with you and slap export controls on the bomb you say you have built. To be clear, I don't think Anthropic has built anything like a bomb, and I don't think export controls on Fable are appropriate. However, following the U.S. Government making this move, many nations, including U.S. allies, saw how the U.S. can suddenly yank their access to AI models. In many capitals around the world, this has spurred discussions on AI sovereignty and how others can ensure uninterrupted access to this critical technology. For decades, semiconductor manufacturing in China made slow progress; once the U.S. moved to limit China’s access, China’s efforts kicked into high gear. Similarly, once China threatened U.S. access to rare earth minerals, U.S. efforts to secure alternatives accelerated. Now that it has become crystal clear that private U.S. companies and the U.S. government can limit, in short order, other nations’ access to frontier AI models, the incentive of others to invest more in alternatives like open source grows significantly. Of course, training frontier models is not easy, so it remains to be seen how successful they are, but we have crossed the rubicon. Satya Nadella wrote an essay about the importance of building a healthy ecosystem on top of frontier AI technology. I heartily agree with him, and hope this week’s events will ultimately prove to be constructive steps toward this. I hope we can build a more free, more open world, where research is freely shared, and laws and societal norms shape a level playing field that allows everyone to make progress. A silver lining of the events of these past two weeks is now that everyone better realizes key points of instability of the current system, we can all work to create a more stable foundation. [Original text: The Batch newsletter]

idees.text_fr: « La mémoire des agents est encore à ses débuts, avec peu ou pas de normes… mais un modèle commun émerge : la mémoire wiki. » C'est ainsi que @hwchase17 (co-fondateur de @LangChain) a récemment décrit l'état actuel de la mémoire des agents. Au cours de la dernière année, j'ai construit deux systèmes distincts qui ont accidentellement convergé vers la même idée. L'un construit des wikis LLM (modèles de langage étendu) par projet à partir de mes notes, recherches et conversations. L'autre sert ma mémoire unifiée via un serveur @fastmcp. Mais je pense que les combiner est la pièce manquante. Aujourd'hui, la plupart des agents IA recherchent à plusieurs reprises les mêmes documents, récupèrent les mêmes fragments et reconstruisent la même compréhension chaque fois que vous posez une question. La mémoire wiki change cette abstraction. Au lieu de raisonner directement sur des documents bruts, l'agent construit progressivement un petit wiki Markdown structuré à partir de votre mémoire unifiée qui devient sa connaissance de travail locale. La première conversation le crée. Chaque conversation suivante l'améliore. C'est un modèle différent du RAG traditionnel. Aujourd'hui, je n'utilise les wikis LLM que pour des projets personnels construits sur mon Second Cerveau. Imaginez maintenant faire la même chose pour les données d'entreprise… Votre mémoire unifiée reste la source de vérité. Le wiki devient une couche légère, spécifique à la tâche, sur laquelle l'agent peut raisonner. @fastmcp (par @PrefectIO) se situe entre les deux. Il gère la logique métier : Recherche dans la mémoire unifiée Construit le wiki Synchronise les sources modifiées Persiste les nouvelles connaissances Le 'harness' appelle simplement ces outils et compétences. Mieux encore, cela ne nécessite pas de GraphRAG sur l'ensemble de votre corpus. Donc vous : Gardez vos sources de données existantes telles quelles (avec ou sans KG) Construisez un wiki local qui implémente un KG léger via des références de fichiers Pointez un agent directement vers le wiki qui utilise la divulgation progressive pour l'interroger Le serveur MCP agit uniquement comme le moteur entre les données de votre entreprise et le wiki LLM. Le problème d'ingénierie le plus difficile est de le maintenir synchronisé. Chaque page sait déjà quels documents sources l'ont créée. Lorsque ces documents changent, seules les pages wiki affectées doivent être mises à jour, tandis que tout le reste continue de consolider sa compréhension. Cela signifie que je peux passer de Claude Code à Codex demain sans changer le fonctionnement de la mémoire. Le wiki reste local. L'intelligence reste derrière le serveur @fastmcp (par @PrefectIO). C'est l'architecture de mémoire à long terme vers laquelle je converge de plus en plus. P.S.
